content: Encouraging individuals to use HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits is an effective way to help them learn their HIV status. The World Health Organization (WHO) does not recommend the use of HIVST kits by parents or guardians to test infants or young children, as these tests are unreliable for children under 18 months due to the potential presence of maternal antibodies. For some individuals, additional HIV testing after one month of starting PrEP may be necessary to confirm the absence of AHI at the time of initiation. Facility-based HIV self-testing (FB-HIVST) has shown promise in certain settings, particularly where HIV testing coverage is suboptimal. Some programs have demonstrated that offering self-test kits at facilities is more effective, simpler, and less costly than risk-based screening tools, which may miss opportunities for testing. During the COVID-19 pandemic, FB-HIVST was widely adopted to maintain essential health services amidst healthcare worker shortages. Despite some uncertainty about its benefits in all settings, FB-HIVST has been found to increase testing uptake, improve equity, and potentially reduce costs. WHO recommends FB-HIVST as an additional approach to facility-based HIV testing, though this recommendation is conditional due to variability in evidence quality and setting-specific factors. In Zimbabwe, a pilot program integrated HIV testing and treatment services into family planning clinics to address high HIV incidence and low service uptake. This model included provider-administered testing and HIVST options for clients and their partners, with self-testing available on-site or for home use. Between October 2020 and December 2022, 18,756 women accessed family planning services, with 7% diagnosed with HIV. Of these, 21% initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) on-site, while others were referred for external services. HIVST kits were used both on-site and privately, with 6% of users reporting reactive results, all of whom confirmed their status through follow-up testing. HIVST has also been explored as a tool to support PrEP delivery. PrEP involves the use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-negative individuals to reduce their risk of acquiring HIV. Despite its proven effectiveness, access to PrEP remains limited due to barriers such as long wait times at health facilities, frequent visits for testing and refills, and stigma. Differentiated PrEP delivery models, including the use of HIVST, can simplify access and improve convenience for clients. HIVST can be used for PrEP initiation, re-initiation after a break, and continuation, with studies showing similar levels of PrEP adherence and refill rates compared to standard testing. Additionally, HIVST-supported PrEP delivery has been found to be cost-effective and acceptable to both clients and providers. Web-based distribution of HIVST kits has also been piloted in Vietnam to improve access for key populations. Clients registered on an online platform to request kits, which could be delivered to their homes or picked up at designated locations. Reactive results were followed up with confirmatory testing and linkage to care. This model demonstrated high client satisfaction and feasibility, with 98% of users reporting satisfaction with the service. The program has since been scaled up to additional provinces, with significant increases in the number of distributed kits and confirmed HIV-positive cases linked to treatment. To optimize HIV testing services, WHO recommends offering a range of testing approaches tailored to local contexts, including facility-based, community-based, network-based, and self-testing services. Providing individuals with choices, such as oral or blood-based self-tests, can increase accessibility and uptake. Flexible service hours and community engagement are also critical for reaching key populations. Self-testing can also be integrated with other health services, such as dual HIV/syphilis testing for pregnant women or self-sampling technologies for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Virtual tools, such as instructional videos and online support, can enhance the self-testing experience, particularly for young people and those seeking discreet options. Ongoing monitoring and evaluation are essential to refine service delivery and maximize impact.
